overview: Awfāt, usually called Ifat, was a Muslim sultanate on the Ethiopian highland escarpment. Excavations distinguish its capital and royal cemetery from other towns, including Nora.

periods.title: A Walasma capital
periods.summary: The Walasma dynasty established itself at Awfāt. Royal inscriptions and a city, citadel and cemetery help locate its political centre.

periods.title: Changing power, inhabited towns
periods.summary: At Nora, successive mosque buildings document an active Muslim town during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Urban occupation and dynastic chronology are different questions.

periods.title: Nora’s later occupation
periods.summary: The excavation synthesis places Nora’s occupation into the first third of the sixteenth century. This extends the town’s history beyond the earlier capital’s political role.

items.text: Nora’s houses used stone and earth mortar, with niches in their walls. Pottery lay on earthen floors. Streets and open spaces connected the buildings.
Unglazed pottery, imported beads and cowries survived at Nora. Iron rods may relate to currency described in medieval texts, but that identification remains a hypothesis.

The 2008 excavations examined houses and two of Nora’s five mosques. The resulting volume studies pottery, glass, metal and animal remains together. A town’s history comes from ordinary discarded material as well as its largest buildings.

Nora had a Great Mosque and four smaller neighbourhood mosques. Their distribution places religious buildings among residential areas. The large congregational building was only one part of the town’s religious landscape.
The Great Mosque changed over time. Earlier stone columns were made from single pieces; a later phase used assembled column elements. Rebuilding altered how the roof was supported.
In the small mosque labelled M2, one central column supported the prayer room. A courtyard lay to the south, while the prayer niche marked its northern side.
A worked stone object near M2 was interpreted as a basin for ritual washing. The interpretation connects an object with preparation for prayer, although its precise use is not directly recorded.
Walasma tomb inscriptions preserve names, religious invocations and dates in the 1360s and 1370s. They provide evidence for the dynasty independent of later narrative histories.

Nora’s occupation is dated broadly from the late thirteenth century to the first third of the sixteenth. That range describes a settlement, not a single ruler’s reign or an exact date when all its inhabitants left.

ending.text: Awfāt probably lost its capital status after 1376. Later warfare brought Christian royal control over Ifat, while the Walasma dynasty continued elsewhere. Disagreements about rulers’ dates and continuing towns make a single universal “fall” date misleading.
